clinicalPearls: An aggressive plasma-cell neoplasm defined by clonal plasma cells circulating in the peripheral blood above the accepted diagnostic threshold
Primary plasma cell leukaemia arises de novo, whereas secondary disease represents leukaemic transformation of pre-existing multiple myeloma
Presents with rapidly progressive disease including anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia and frequent extramedullary involvement
Circulating plasma cells often express CD38 and CD138 but characteristically lack CD56, which is more typical of marrow-confined myeloma
High-risk cytogenetic abnormalities, including deletion 17p and translocations involving MYC, are common and contribute to the poor prognosis
Treatment relies on intensive combination regimens incorporating proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory agents and anti-CD38 targeted therapy, with autologous HSCT in eligible patients
Diagnosis requires prompt recognition, as the disease can deteriorate quickly with hyperviscosity, renal failure and tumour lysis
reference.pathophysiology: Plasma cell leukaemia is characterised by a clone of malignant plasma cells that has lost the marrow-retention signals of ordinary myeloma and circulates freely in the blood, reflecting altered adhesion-molecule expression such as reduced CD56. Primary disease arises without an antecedent plasma-cell disorder, while secondary disease evolves from progressive multiple myeloma. The clone frequently harbours high-risk genomic changes, including TP53 loss through deletion 17p and MYC rearrangements, driving proliferation, genomic instability and extramedullary dissemination. Widespread infiltration of blood, marrow and extramedullary sites produces the profound cytopenias, end-organ damage and monoclonal protein burden that define the aggressive clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple myeloma with a small circulating plasma-cell component
Reactive plasmacytosis from severe infection or systemic illness
Metastatic carcinoma with a leukaemic blood picture
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film and flow cytometry to quantify and immunophenotype circulating clonal plasma cells
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics and FISH for high-risk abnormalities
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains
Renal function, calcium, and markers of tumour lysis
Beta-2 microglobulin, lactate dehydrogenase and albumin for prognostic assessment
Imaging for bone disease and extramedullary plasmacytomas
redFlags: Acute kidney injury from light-chain nephropathy or hypercalcaemia
Hyperviscosity with neurological or visual disturbance
Symptomatic hypercalcaemia or tumour lysis syndrome
Cord compression or extramedullary mass with neurological deficit
Profound cytopenias causing bleeding or life-threatening infection
reference.prognosis: Plasma cell leukaemia carries a markedly worse prognosis than multiple myeloma, with shorter survival despite modern therapy; secondary disease is particularly aggressive, and outcomes are best when intensive combination treatment and autologous HSCT can be delivered to eligible patients.
pitfalls: Underestimating circulating plasma cells and missing the diagnosis when the burden is only modestly elevated
Assuming the CD56 positivity typical of marrow myeloma, which is often absent in leukaemic disease
Delaying treatment of hypercalcaemia, renal failure or tumour lysis
Applying standard myeloma prognostic assumptions to a much more aggressive disease
Failing to identify high-risk cytogenetics that alter management and outlook
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on plasma cell disorders
management: Treatment intent is rapid, reliable disease control rather than watch and wait, since this is an ultrahigh-risk form of multiple myeloma with circulating clonal plasma cells.
Induction typically uses a multiagent combination rather than a single agent or two drug approach.
Induction commonly combines a proteasome inhibitor, an immunomodulatory agent, and a corticosteroid, often with an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody added.
Eligible patients are consolidated with autologous stem cell transplantation; allogeneic transplantation is considered only in selected younger, fit patients given its higher toxicity.
Maintenance therapy after transplant or after induction in transplant-ineligible patients is used to try to sustain remission.

There is no role for surgery or radiotherapy as primary treatment of the leukaemic clone, though localized radiotherapy or surgical fixation may still be used for symptomatic bone lesions, cord compression, or a dominant extramedullary mass.

Relapsed disease options extrapolated from myeloma management include dexamethasone or intravenous methylprednisolone for palliation, melphalan-based regimens, bendamustine alone or with other myeloma agents, addition of panobinostat to a proteasome inhibitor, bortezomib with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, and anthracycline-based combination regimens for refractory disease with good performance status.
Bone disease is managed with bone-targeted therapy such as a bisphosphonate or denosumab, plus radiotherapy or surgical fixation for a focal or impending fracture.
Anaemia is managed with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent or transfusion when symptomatic and not responding to other measures.

Infection prevention includes vaccination, antibacterial prophylaxis around initial treatment, antiviral prophylaxis with proteasome inhibitor or anti-CD38 therapy, and Pneumocystis prophylaxis during prolonged steroid or anti-CD38 therapy.
Hypercalcaemia is treated with aggressive hydration and an intravenous bisphosphonate, managed as an emergency when severe.
Spinal cord compression is treated with corticosteroids and radiotherapy, with chemotherapy or surgical decompression considered in selected patients.

Monitor circulating plasma cell count, paraprotein or free light chains, blood counts, and renal function closely given how quickly this disease can change, with high-risk cytogenetics informing prognosis.

Any suspected or confirmed case should be referred promptly to haemato-oncology for combination treatment planning and transplant eligibility assessment, given the risk of acute complications such as renal failure, hypercalcaemia, hyperviscosity, cord compression, and tumour lysis.
